newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan, HK avoid clash over ships' flags.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan, HK avoid clash over ships' flags.

text.p: Hong Kong and Taiwan side-stepped a conflict over shipping flags on Saturday, agreeing to fly no national flags on their vessels when they visit each other's ports after the British colony returns to Chinese rule.
A memorandum signed after more than six hours of talks will let direct shipping links continue after July 1, negotiators told a news briefing.
Taiwan's transport ministry hailed the talks as a success, describing the conclusion as "satisfactory."
"This is the best available solution at the moment," the ministry said through state-funded Central News Agency.

But analysts warned that the compromise by the Hong Kong side could be an offensive by Taiwan's rival China to pave the way for future direct links between the Nationalist island and the Communist mainland.
Beijing-appointed Hong Kong negotiator George Chao said the agreement was a temporary solution.
"Hong Kong is a special administrative region. We will fly the bauhinia flag. And because you (Taiwan) don't have such (identification) flag, Taiwan temporarily would not fly the flag," he said.
He said the sides would eventually work out a solution for the Taiwan flag problem, but he did not give a specific time.
"The resolution can help resolve the shipping problem between Taiwan and Hong Kong, preventing politicisation of the issue," said Chao, chairman of the Hong Kong Shipowners Association.

Hong Kong is an important transit point for more than $30 billion in investments that has poured into China from Taiwan since the easing of unofficial ties between Beijing and Taipei in the late 1980s.

But Beijing, which regards Nationalist Taiwan as a renegade province, objects to any ship entering Hong Kong harbour flying the flag of the exiled Republic of China, which took refuge on Taiwan after its 1949 civil war defeat by the Communists.
It also rejected the island's proposal that the sides lower their flags while entering each other's port.
Taiwan said it would not admit Hong Kong ships under the Communists' five-star flag unless its own ships were permitted to fly the Nationalist flag.

They had failed to find a compromise during a first round of talks in Hong Kong on May 2. If a deal had not been struck direct shipping between them could have been suspended at midnight on June 30, when Hong Kong is handed back to China by Britain.

Taiwan's chief negotiator Chang Liang-jen, deputy secretary-general of the quasi-official Straits Exchange Foundation, said Saturday's talks would be a good beginning in the relations between Taiwan and Hong Kong.
"The present arrangement meets our policy, and also the requirement of Hong Kong," he said in a news briefing, adding it benefits both sides economically.
Political analysts, however, cautioned Taiwan authorities, saying the compromise from the Hong Kong side could be China's "united front ploy."

"The agreement appears to be a concession from the mainland side. The Communists apparently hopes to use this to please Taiwan shippers and businessmen, and pave the way for future direct links with Taiwan," said National Taiwan University law professor Hu Fu.
